correctness.rationale: The explicit bounded bilinear product has norm bound sqrt(m); T_m is onto with a concrete isometric right inverse, its kernel has dimension m−1, and A_m²=ell¹ by coefficientwise factorization. For every other orthonormal natural basis, unitary-column products lie in ker T_m, forcing tail monomiality and a head unitary Q with Q^tQ diagonal; removing square-root phases makes Q real orthogonal. Conversely all R in O(m) work. Every universal assertion is proved analytically, with exact finite-coordinate checks serving only as corroboration.

evidence: Cadavid–Rodriguez–Vidal, arXiv:2311.08387v2, Section 3.2, Example 3.6, explicitly has e_(2j−1)^2=e_(2j)^2=e_(2j)+e_(2j+1).
The span of these pair-sums has an infinite-dimensional orthogonal complement, so the Example 3.6 square is not dense.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The published Hilbert examples prove failure of uniqueness without the dense-square premise. Even the existence of orthogonal basis rotations does not imply onto-ness or dense square, because their squares have infinitely many independent linear relations. The present family has a bounded onto linear evolution operator and finite-dimensional kernel, and it classifies all orthonormal natural bases.

value.rationale: The explicit open question asks if dense square forces basis uniqueness. These examples answer no even with stronger onto evolution operator, yield exact complete O(m)/signed-permutation moduli for every finite kernel defect, and identify injectivity on ell¹ as a clear sufficient boundary, with defect 1 already allowing failure. The structural classification is not merely a single cheap negative test.
